ai.definition: Direct Air Capture at Scale is a technology that captures carbon dioxide directly from the ambient air and stores it permanently or reuses it. This process can be used to remove greenhouse gases from the atmosphere and mitigate climate change.
ai.howItWorks: Large fans push air through solid sorbents or liquid solvents, which capture CO2. Heat is then applied to release a concentrated stream of CO2 that can be stored underground in mineralized form.
ai.problemSolved: Direct Air Capture at Scale addresses the issue of hard-to-abate emissions by providing a method for removing carbon dioxide directly from the atmosphere on a large scale.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves creating and scaling up the equipment used to capture CO2, including large fans, sorbents, solvents, and heating systems. The materials need to be durable and efficient in capturing CO2.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes designing the air capture units, selecting appropriate sorbents or solvents, setting up the necessary infrastructure for heat application, and integrating the system into a larger carbon removal network.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the initial capital investment for equipment, operational costs such as energy consumption for heating, and maintenance costs. The efficiency of sorbent/solvent materials also significantly impacts cost.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is promising but faces challenges in scaling up and reducing costs to make it economically viable on a large scale.
ai.regulation: Current regulatory frameworks vary widely, with some regions offering incentives for carbon removal technologies. However, there are no standardized regulations yet for direct air capture at scale.
ai.risks: Technical risks include the efficiency of CO2 capture and storage, potential environmental impacts from mineralization processes, and the risk of scaling up without adequate testing.
ai.profitability: Profitability is currently low due to high costs and limited market demand. However, as regulations around carbon emissions become stricter, there could be increased incentives for investment in this technology.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development may focus on improving capture efficiency, reducing operational costs, and developing more sustainable materials for sorbents and solvents.

glossary.def: A process that extracts carbon dioxide directly from the ambient air.
A material used to capture CO2 from the air or gas streams.
A liquid used in a process to dissolve and capture CO2 for later release and storage.

subsystems.name: Air contactor
subsystems.role: moves ambient air past a material that captures carbon dioxide.
parts: sorbent-coated contactor sheets or solvent-filled packing

subsystems.name: Regeneration unit
subsystems.role: releases the captured CO2 and regenerates the capture material for reuse.

subsystems.name: CO2 compression and purification
subsystems.role: turns the released gas into a concentrated stream ready for transport.

subsystems.name: Energy system
subsystems.role: supplies the heat and electricity the plant needs without adding new CO2.

buildSteps.title: Choose a site
buildSteps.detail: Look for abundant low-carbon energy, suitable geology for permanent storage, and enough land for large air contactors.

buildSteps.title: Design the contactor
buildSteps.detail: Engineers size the fan array and sorbent area to capture a target tonnage of CO2 per year from air that is only about 0.04% CO2.

buildSteps.title: Manufacture contactor modules
buildSteps.detail: Contactor sheets or packing are produced in factories, then shipped to site for assembly.

buildSteps.title: Build regeneration and compression plant
buildSteps.detail: Heat exchangers, vacuum vessels and compressors are assembled and connected to the contactors.

buildSteps.title: Drill storage wells
buildSteps.detail: Wells are drilled into deep saline aquifers or basalt formations, then tested for injectivity.

buildSteps.title: Connect clean energy
buildSteps.detail: The plant is wired to nearby wind, solar or geothermal sources, often with batteries or thermal storage to smooth supply.

buildSteps.title: Commission and monitor
buildSteps.detail: The plant is started up, capture rate is measured, and underground CO2 plumes are tracked with seismic and well sensors.

prerequisites.why: direct air capture is energy-hungry; running it on fossil energy would emit more CO2 than it removes.
materials must capture CO2 from very dilute air and survive many thousands of cycles without degrading.
pipelines, injection wells and monitoring are proven in some regions but not widespread.
deep saline aquifers and basalt formations can hold CO2 permanently, but capacity is mapped unevenly.
to reach gigatonne scale, contactors must be mass-produced cheaply, much like solar panels or cars.

pathway.milestone: Pilot plants capturing thousands of tonnes per year, such as Climeworks' Orca and Mammoth in Iceland, with CO2 injected into basalt for mineralisation (CarbFix).
pathway.unlocks: proof that the full chain—capture, compression, injection and monitoring—works.

pathway.milestone: Megatonne-scale hubs, for example 1PointFive's Stratos project in Texas, using dedicated storage.
pathway.unlocks: economies of scale and learning by doing.

pathway.milestone: Gigatonne-scale deployment using mass-manufactured contactors and shared CO2 pipelines.
Integration with synthetic fuel production or permanent storage in basalt and saline aquifers worldwide.
pathway.unlocks: a carbon removal industry comparable in size to today's fossil fuel industry.
